parts.title: Building and Checking a Computer Model of Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementia in the United States (MICROSIM)
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We urgently need ways to prevent or slow down Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD). These are groups of diseases that affect memory and thinking, and they are a major cause of death and disability in older people. Managing blood pressure (BP), the pressure of blood against the walls of our blood vessels, is a promising way to help. Yet we do not know how different ways of controlling BP affect AD/ADRD across a person's whole life. Randomized controlled trials, which are studies that randomly assign people to receive a treatment or not, may not be possible here. They would need to follow people for a very long time and include huge numbers of people.

Simulation analysis is a practical way to estimate these effects using the best data we have. It works by building a computer model that follows each person through their life, and then adds up what happens across everyone. However, the simulation tools we already have cannot estimate how BP control affects both dementia and heart and blood vessel disease.

In this paper, we describe how we designed MICROSIM (short for Michigan Chronic Disease Simulation Model), a new simulation tool for the whole population. We also explain how we built it and how we checked it against real data. MICROSIM is a population health microsimulation: it follows each person through their life and then adds up the results for the whole population. We built it to study how lower blood pressure over the life course affects late-life thinking and memory in Blacks, Hispanics, and Whites. We call this study the BP-COG study.

MICROSIM is a computer program that follows individual people, and it uses a Monte Carlo simulation. In this kind of simulation, the computer runs a very large number of random steps, each with its own chance of happening, to see how the results could vary. We designed it following the best practices for building computer code.

MICROSIM estimates each person's yearly levels of risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease, and the chances of moving from one outcome to another. It does this for all-cause dementia, stroke, heart attack and death, using a sample of US adults 18 and older that is representative of the whole country. The sample comes from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), a large national health survey.

We built MICROSIM from changes in risk factors over time, and from changes in thinking and memory, using changes from a combined dataset of results from 6 US studies that followed people forward in time. We estimated heart and blood vessel risks with a widely used risk model. We worked out the effects of BP treatment from meta-analyses, which are studies that combine the results of many randomized trials.

MICROSIM is open-source, meaning anyone can see and change its code. It is extensible, which means we can add new features to it. We designed it to estimate how different ways of managing BP affect the whole population. It also reproduces US estimates of BP and other risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease, how these change over time, and new cases of all-cause dementia, stroke, heart attack and death.
parts.introduction_first: Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) are major causes of death and disability in older people. Preventing or delaying them can help people live longer, stay less disabled, need fewer nursing homes, spend less on health care, and live better lives. Managing blood pressure (BP) is a promising way to prevent AD/ADRD. It is also a key part of preventing heart and blood vessel disease, both in the early stages and in the later stages, which includes stroke and a heart attack. Little is known about how BP treatment affects all-cause heart and blood vessel disease and AD/ADRD together across the whole population.
parts.introduction_rest:
Over the past 20 years, more and more evidence has led to important new clinical guidelines for treating people more aggressively when they have risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease that can be changed. Most of the policy assessments and simulation models behind these new guidelines look only at how blood pressure affects heart and blood vessel disease. They do not look at how it affects AD/ADRD [1–4]. Yet blood pressure is a strong risk factor for AD/ADRD. If clinicians and policymakers think about how BP affects AD/ADRD and other diseases, it may change how they define what "optimal" means for BP treatment.

Here is one example. Lowering BP to the best levels (below 120/80 mm Hg, a standard way of describing blood pressure) reduces the number of heart and blood vessel events. It also reduces mild cognitive impairment (MCI), which is a mild difficulty with thinking and memory. In people with a high risk of heart and blood vessel disease, it also reduces the combination of MCI and AD/ADRD [5, 6]. However, this group in the US is fairly small.

We do not know whether lowering BP to the best levels also reduces heart and blood vessel disease and AD/ADRD in the larger group of adults at lower risk of heart and blood vessel disease. One example is a group of Black people aged 55 who have a blood pressure of 130–139 mm Hg. If treating BP more strongly early in life has a large effect on thinking and memory in later life and on AD/ADRD, then the best time to start BP treatment, the best level to aim for, and the best level to aim for should all shift earlier and more strongly. In the same way, we can estimate how much BP treatment matters on its own, separately from other factors, for heart and blood vessel disease compared with AD/ADRD. This may help us describe more accurately how different BP treatment policies affect quality of life, cost-effectiveness (whether a treatment gives good health benefits for its cost), and the benefit to society. That knowledge can then guide the best policy.

Large randomized controlled trials are the least biased way to estimate how BP treatment affects AD/ADRD, but they may not be possible. The most effective and practical approach for now may be simulation analysis. It uses evidence from published risk models, from meta-analyses of randomized trials, and from the best available observational data, which are studies that follow people without assigning them to a group.

There are microsimulation models of heart and blood vessel disease and of dementia, but none of them do for both. In this paper, we describe how we designed a new population health microsimulation tool, MICROSIM (short for Michigan Chronic Disease Simulation Model), and how we built and checked it against real data. We built it to study how lower blood pressure over the life course affects thinking and memory in late life. We call it the BP-COG study, short for the effect of BP levels over the life course on cognitive decline and dementia.

We designed MICROSIM by following the best practices for building computer code. We built it from a new simulation model of heart and blood vessel disease and AD/ADRD. Our first research purpose was to explore a series of questions about how different ways of managing BP affect thinking and memory in late life and all-cause dementia, and how race differences in the number of all-cause dementia cases play out. Our final research purpose is to build a tool that can be extended to a wide range of questions about managing long-lasting diseases, as new medical conditions are added.
parts.discussion:
Discussion

In this paper, we describe how we built a new simulation tool for the whole population, called MICROSIM, that follows people through their lives and then adds up what happens across everyone. It is a microsimulation, which means it follows each person one at a time. MICROSIM is extensible, meaning we can add new features to it. It is open-source, meaning anyone can see and change its code. It was first designed to explore how heart and blood vessel disease and thinking and memory change when people are treated for blood pressure in different ways. The key parts of the tool that we need to reach those goals check well against standards for the whole population. We also designed the tool so that it is fairly easy to change, for example by switching on a particular risk model. We can also extend it to add more outcomes, or to change how the results are organized, for example to include more of the outcomes that matter in clinical care.

In its current version, MICROSIM has the parts needed to answer a set of research questions about risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease, how to manage those risk factors, heart and blood vessel disease, dementia, and quality of life. It is fairly easy to change slightly to answer a range of related questions. One example is to predict future heart and blood vessel disease and dementia under different risk assumptions, or under different definitions of heart and blood vessel disease and dementia. Another is to work out how much BP treatment is worth, both with and without counting the effects on thinking and memory. Perhaps even more important, the tool can be extended. That opens the door to looking more fully at other diseases, such as congestive heart failure (when the heart cannot keep enough blood flowing to the body), peripheral vascular disease (disease of the blood vessels in the body's outer parts, such as the legs and feet), and chronic kidney disease (long-lasting damage to the kidneys). It also opens the door to risk markers, such as social determinants of health, meaning things like income, education and social support that shape health. It opens the door to treatments, such as statins (medicines that lower cholesterol) and oral hypoglycemics (medicines that lower blood sugar). And it opens the door to public health actions that matter for health, such as access to healthy food and green spaces. With these extensions, the simulation could answer a huge range of research questions.

In ongoing work, we are also building ways to simulate clinical trials easily, and to add information about the people in each disease. In particular, we are extending the simulation to study how people manage risk factors after a stroke. For this, we include the type of stroke, the subtypes of ischemic stroke (a stroke caused by a blockage in the blood vessels), and how severe the stroke is.

MICROSIM's main strengths are that we built it following the best practices for building computer code, that we used the best data we could to work out the core assumptions of the simulation, and that we checked its core parts against real data. As far as we know, using programming best practices is fairly unusual for a simulation built by researchers. We believe this will give us a codebase that is reliable enough to draw accurate conclusions about the whole population.

MICROSIM's main limitations are that, as with any simulation, its results can only be as strong as the core assumptions of the model. Because the tool is so complex, it relies on many assumptions that are hard to test directly with the evidence we have today, such as how BP treatment affects thinking and memory. As stronger evidence comes in, we intend to keep adding the best available evidence to MICROSIM. In the same way, the way the tool is built assumes fairly simple relationships, even though the real world may be more complex. For example, the link between lower blood pressure and the chance of dying may not follow a straight line. Instead, it may follow a J-shaped curve, where fewer people die at low blood pressure, then more die as blood pressure rises. So, to use MICROSIM for a particular research question, we will need to think about how those assumptions may affect the results.

When an uncertain assumption could plausibly change the conclusions, we could run robust sensitivity analyses. These are checks in which we change the assumptions and see how much the results change. We also included race in the regression models that underlie MICROSIM. A regression model is a statistical tool that estimates how one thing, such as dementia, changes with another, such as race. However, the data used to build these models were often not enough to answer the effects of Hispanic ethnicity, for example on dementia. So, although the model includes Hispanic people, it is not clear that MICROSIM would reproduce US estimates of outcomes for Hispanic people.

## How we checked the model, and what it showed

### How we checked the model

We wanted to find the key things that would most likely affect how well our model matches high-quality data. That data was not used to build the model for our main features and central research questions. For these key things, we first worked out the best way to check the model. The main features we focused on were four: how well the model represents the whole population, how risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease change over time, how often people have new cases of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and how often people have new cases of dementia. ASCVD means heart and blood vessel disease caused by a buildup of fatty deposits in the arteries.

### Checking the model against a simulated population [48]

Table 2 compares two simulated populations from MICROSIM with published data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). The first is a simulated population of 500,000 people, chosen at random. The second is a published population of 500,000 people from the 2007–2010 NHANES survey. The survey gives each person a weight, which reflects how much they count toward the national totals.

The two simulated populations matched almost exactly. The 500,000 people in MICROSIM had the same ages, races, ethnicities, and average values as the published group. The two also matched very well in their risk factor levels. We counted someone as having high blood pressure (hypertension) if their blood pressure was above 140/90 mmHg or if they were taking medicine to lower their blood pressure. The published group was the same size, and the two matched in their risk factor levels.

### Checking the model against risk factor levels over time [51]

We found that the simulation closely reproduced the changes in risk factor levels over time that were actually seen in the real BP COG groups (results not shown). However, this finding is somewhat circular, because those groups were used to build the simulation's models. So we wanted a more reliable test of how well the simulation follows these changes.

To do this, we compared a simulated population that follows people forward in time with a "pseudo-cohort" from the NHANES. A pseudo-cohort is a stand-in group that is built from repeated NHANES surveys, each looking at people at a single point in time. We built a simulated population of 250,000 adults 18 or older that is representative of the whole country. It had no history of stroke, heart attack, or dementia. We started it in 1999, using NHANES data from that year, and then moved it forward for 18 years until 2017, the most recent year for which NHANES data were available.

Next, we removed the simulated people who died before 2017. For the NHANES comparison, we included adults aged 36 or older. We started at age 18 and moved forward 18 years. We left out adults who had moved into the US, because the simulation does not include people moving in or out.

Figure 2 shows the results. It is a histogram, a bar chart that shows how many people fall into each range of a measurement. It compares the risk factor levels in the simulated population, which started in 1999 and was moved forward 18 years, with the levels in the pseudo-cohort, which was the NHANES population in 2017 without people moving in.

The simulation generally closely matched both the typical level and the spread of risk factor levels. The one exception was that it predicted diastolic blood pressure too high. The simulated average was 78.7 mmHg, compared with 71.6 mmHg in the pseudo-cohort. The standard deviation, which shows how widely values are spread around the average, was 9.2 mmHg in the simulation and 10.9 mmHg in the pseudo-cohort. The simulation also slightly underestimated the spread of total cholesterol. The simulated average was 200.0 mg/dL, compared with 196.8 mg/dL in the pseudo-cohort. The standard deviation was 31.0 mg/dL in the simulation and 41.3 mg/dL in the pseudo-cohort.

### Checking how often people have new cases of ASCVD and how often they die [52]

Table 3 sums up the estimated yearly rate of new cases of stroke and heart attack in a simulated population of 250,000 people from 1999 to 2015, run by MICROSIM. We report this rate per 100,000 people, adjusted for age. This means we compared people of different ages, so that differences in age do not distort the comparison.

In the simulation, the yearly rate of new heart attacks was 234 per 100,000 people. The 95% confidence interval was 232 to 241. A confidence interval is a range that shows how uncertain an estimate is. The simulation started in 1999.

MICROSIM's yearly rate of new heart attacks is broadly similar to the rate seen in the Kaiser Permanente population. That population had between 208 and 284 new cases per 100,000 people from 1999 to 2008 [53]. The yearly rate of new strokes was 153 per 100,000 people in the simulation. This falls within the range of rates reported in population studies over the same years, which ranged from 130 to 400 per 100,000 people [54–56]. The rate of new hospital admissions was around 200 per 100,000 people [57].

When we compare people of the same age, Black people generally have about twice as many new strokes as White people [55, 56]. In the simulation, the yearly rate of new strokes was 243 per 100,000 people in Black people and 123 per 100,000 people in White people. Overall, the simulation estimated 699 new cases of death per 100,000 people, compared with 729 in population-level estimates. After we adjusted the simulation to match the US national life tables, it reproduced the chance of dying at each age (Fig 3). ### Checking the effects of treatment [59]

To find out whether the simulation reproduced how BP treatment affects people in real life, we ran 15 simulations. Each one moved a population of 150,000 people forward for 18 years and older, with no history of dementia, stroke, or heart attack, using NHANES data.

We ran two versions. In the "as-treated" version, BP treatment follows current practice, which is usual care. In the other version, every person gets a single BP medicine added to their current treatment. On average, this lowered blood pressure by 5.5 mmHg and 3.1 mmHg.

The simulation estimated that the relative risk of new stroke was 0.76, with a range of 0.72 to 0.82. The relative risk of new heart attack was 0.85, with a range of 0.81 to 0.89. A relative risk compares how likely a person is to have a condition with how likely they are to have it in the untreated group. These estimates are close to the standard we used to build the simulation. That standard comes from a meta-analysis of trials that lowered blood pressure, which found a relative risk of 0.79 for new stroke and a relative risk of 0.87 for new heart attack [60].

### Checking how often people have new cases of dementia [61]

We built a population of 200,000 people, representative of the whole country, from NHANES. It included people aged 18 and older with no history of dementia, stroke, or heart attack. We moved the simulation forward for 20 years and estimated how often people had new cases of all-cause dementia.

Figure 4 compares the all-cause dementia rate from MICROSIM with the age-dementia rate from the Brookmeyer et al. meta-analysis [42]. The two closely matched across all ages.

New cases of dementia by age in the simulated population, compared with the age-dementia rates from the Brookmeyer et al. meta-analysis [33].

### Showing how a combined model could help

One strength of MICROSIM is that it combines two kinds of model. It follows individual people, and it also follows the whole population. This lets us estimate things that would usually need different kinds of study.

For example, a common type of study is a fixed probability decision analysis. It uses a fixed chance of each outcome, such as a fixed chance of getting a certain BP treatment, to estimate the average effect across the population. (For example, it can show how many quality-adjusted life years are gained compared with usual care.) A quality-adjusted life year is a year of healthy life, adjusted for how well people are doing. In the same way, a regression-based analysis of a cohort study can estimate how much the results vary between different BP treatment plans and how much they vary within the same plan. A regression-based analysis is a statistical method that estimates how much each factor is linked to an outcome. MICROSIM's design lets us estimate both kinds of variation, and also how the two vary together.

We wanted to show how this combined approach can describe effects across the population, effects for single people, and effects split by the factors we are interested in. So we ran two simple models. The first compared a group of 300,000 people aged 18 or older who had high blood pressure at the start and no history of dementia, stroke, or heart attack. They were treated with usual care. The second used a similar group of 300,000 people with high blood pressure at the start, treated with intensive BP control based on the Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT) [5].

The simulation estimated that intensive BP control gained a small amount of quality-adjusted life years across the population, 20.9 compared with 20.8. This is similar to what a fixed probability decision analysis would give. However, we also found that the average gain in quality-adjusted life years differed from person to person (Fig 5).

We split people into four equal-sized groups, called quartiles, from lowest to highest baseline blood pressure. In the lowest quartile, people with the lowest baseline BP had the same gain: 32.2 quality-adjusted life years in both groups. In the highest quartile, people with the highest baseline BP gained a much larger amount: 13.7 compared with 13.4.

The spread of values within each of these groups (Fig 6) shows that the small differences in average gain between groups make up only a very small part of the overall variation in people's gains. This is similar to what a regression-based analysis of a cohort study would give.

Abbreviations: QALY, quality adjusted life year. SPRINT, Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial. Intensive blood pressure control was based on the Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT-based Algorithm).

Fig 6

The spread of lifetime quality-adjusted life years in the simulation, for people in each quartile of baseline systolic blood pressure, compared with usual care.

Abbreviations: QALY, quality adjusted life year. SPRINT, Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial. Intensive blood pressure control was based on the Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT-based Algorithm).
parts.methods:
## Methods

### What we set out to do, and the specific questions that drove it

Building MICROSIM follows the best practices for systems science research, the field that studies how whole systems work together. The main purpose of MICROSIM is to use data collected in the past to judge how much future population-level BP control could prevent heart and blood vessel events, dementia, and racial disparities (unequal health care and resources between groups of people). Existing population simulations tackle parts of these questions. But we do not know of any simulation that tackles all of them at once, and none of them can account for the trade-off between heart and blood vessel disease and dementia.

Several specific research questions led us to design MICROSIM. First, better BP control leads to less decline in thinking and memory and a lower risk of dementia at a given age. But it also leads to a longer life, because people avoid heart and blood vessel events. Yet age is the main risk factor for dementia and for death from non-cardiovascular causes, such as stroke. So how do these effects balance out? Does BP treatment lower the risk of dementia across the whole life course, or mostly delay it? Second, does the large relative effect of BP treatment on dementia translate into a meaningful effect in years of life lived without dementia? Third, how do these patterns differ by race? Black people have more dementia than white people, but they also have more stroke. Does stronger BP control make the gap between the two groups worse, because stroke prevention lets more people live longer?

These questions are about the population as a whole. We also wanted to describe how people differ from one another. For example, how does the benefit of BP treatment vary with people's starting levels of heart and blood vessel disease and dementia, and with different life courses?

MICROSIM was first designed to answer these specific questions. We designed it to be as open as possible, to keep the code accurate, and to be extensible, so that we can add new questions about managing long-lasting diseases.

### Why we chose a simulation approach

Randomized controlled trials are the best design for finding out how different ways of controlling BP affect thinking and memory and heart and blood vessel disease together. These ways include how strong the treatment is, when it starts, and how patients are chosen. However, designing trials for these questions is hard. Ideally, we would want evidence from large, long-running trials to study how BP and BP treatment across the whole life course affect thinking and memory in late life and dementia. But such trials would be at best cumbersome and costly, and at worst impossible. They would need enormous numbers of people, careful tracking of every person, and a very close match between the treatment and what actually happens. They would also take decades to run, and meaningful results would likely be decades off. During that time, the way treatment is done may have changed so much that the results no longer matter.

Even if we could solve these problems, these trials would not tell us much about patient care in the near term. Shorter trials are easier to run. But they cannot directly show how short-term treatment decisions affect long-term outcomes, because we would have to make assumptions about how much short-term measures matter, or have to stretch our results from higher-risk to lower-risk groups.

Simulation analysis can capture how key trade-offs between people's own lives change over time. It may therefore offer guidance when clinical trials are not possible, and when we are waiting for the results of better, long-running trials for important clinical questions. Simulations can combine the strengths of the best data sources. First, they can use the best available data that follow people over time, to account for complicated natural histories and for competing risks. Second, they can use the best estimates of how well treatment works. When trials exist, they use trial results; when trials do not, they use the best estimates from observational studies, which are studies that follow people without assigning them to a group. This lets them credibly account for a range of treatment effects. With these strengths, simulations may be the best tools for estimating long-term treatment effects, especially in low-risk groups. Simulations can also act as "policy laboratories": they explore what clinical and policy actions mean for society, and they can show how likely such actions are to bring a given benefit.

Yet simulations have several limitations. Because they are so complex, they often seem like "black box science": we cannot easily see how the computer reaches its results, and people often worry about how accurate the results are. Also, most current models are built separately and do not build on one another. This limits progress and may make accuracy worries grow. Building the framework for an effective simulation can be complicated, slow, and require carefully weighing many individual decisions. Careful attention to the inputs to the model is critical when designing the agent-based simulation described below.

Our design for two simulations at once, one for people and one for the population, rests on one idea. A single set of computer code that answers several scientific questions is more efficient and likely to give more reliable results than several simulations for separate questions. This design has three specific advantages. First, it makes it fairly simple to judge the effects of BP treatment on people and on the population, and to describe them in fine detail. For example, if we want to know how BP treatment affects the population, a Markov-based simulation would be well suited to that task. A Markov-based simulation tracks how people move from one state to another, such as from healthy to heart and blood vessel disease, and then from that state to another outcome. It takes the ranges of values for each population feature as its inputs. If we wanted to know how people differ in their outcomes (for example, how BP treatment affects people with different starting BP levels), we could also change that model to follow people at different starting BP levels. But extending that model to other differences between people would take a lot of effort. Examples include the effect of BP treatment at different ages, starting BP levels, blood sugar levels, and other treatments. Our approach estimates a wide variety of effects on people and on the population without changing the core code. It does this by keeping roughly the same patterns of how people with different risk factors are linked to one another.

Second, the code is reusable and easy to change, so we can address a broad range of questions. Besides measuring how BP treatment affects people and the population in race differences in late-life thinking and memory and dementia, our project also has a second goal: to explore possible clinical trial designs that would test how BP treatment affects late-life thinking and memory and dementia. We can directly reuse the main MICROSIM code to run simulations of trials. In a separate part of MICROSIM [9], we have built a simple codebase for trials and trial groups. It lets us run simulated trials inside MICROSIM and pull out the data it needs for analysis. For example, we could run simulated trials of different BP-lowering strategies in different populations, chosen by their starting levels of heart and blood vessel disease and dementia. This would show which groups lead to the most efficient trials. In the same way, we could explore how trial population features, such as size and starting levels of heart and blood vessel disease and dementia, interact with how long trials last, given that the risk of dementia does not rise in a straight line with age.

Third, the inputs to the simulation fit well with existing data and ideas from epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread and how they are studied in populations. The aim behind our questions is to estimate how a person changes over time, and then add up the results for the population. This is the same basic idea behind cohort studies, which follow the same people over time. The main downside of this approach is that it needs a lot of coding and computing time compared with simpler modeling approaches. Here, we describe how we built our simulation of heart and blood vessel disease and dementia for people and for the population, and we try to reduce some of the general limitations that simulation analysis faces.

### Principles for designing simulations

We build simulations by writing computer code that holds the simulation logic and the random steps needed to create the data. These codebases are often large, with tens of thousands of lines of computer code or more. As codebases grow, so does the expected number of bugs [10]. To make sure simulations give accurate and reliable results, we need sound software development processes, so that the code carries out the simulation logic well enough. To do this, we developed a set of principles and strategies based on the best practices for computer programming: openness, readability, simplicity, testing, and validation [11]. We hope that designing a simulation with these principles will make it more reliable and accurate. We also hope that a framework that can be extended and adapted to many long-lasting disease management problems will let researchers build on it to make later analyses as reliable and valid as possible.

Openness: other groups may look at our code, which encourages coders to program carefully and make sure the code is readable and makes sense. The entire MICROSIM codebase [12] is publicly available on GitHub [12]. This includes the notebooks we used to build MICROSIM's inputs and the notebooks we used to check it [13] in this paper. Sharing the code with other researchers also widens the audience. That makes it more likely that we will find errors in the simulation and that others can repeat our work.

Readability: the more readable the code, the less likely it is that errors will appear. We used three main strategies to do this. First, we hired a software developer with industry experience (coauthor LC, Ann Arbor, MI) to help with coding and the software development methods. Second, we developed the core parts of the simulation in pairs, with two coders (JB and LC) sitting side by side and sharing a keyboard to work on key simulation parts. Third, we used automatic formatting tools (Black [14]) that ran when a file was saved, giving the code a consistent and predictable style that makes it easier to read and write.

Simplicity: whenever possible, we used the simplest possible model structures and assumptions. The simpler the logic to be built, the less likely it would be to contain errors. We meant this principle to apply both to the simulation code and to the overall structure of the simulation. At the code level, this principle is mostly a statement of priorities. If a fairly simple data structure can represent the data, we should prefer it over a more complex one. In the same way, although more complex statistical models may represent the data structure a little better, unless they bring major gains in performance, simpler models should be preferred, because they are less likely to contain errors.

Testing: in a large codebase, a change in one area may have unintended effects elsewhere. To reduce this risk, we used unit tests, which check small pieces of code on their own, in a mostly test-driven development approach [15]. For a new piece of code or a bug fix, we first wrote a test that would fail until the code was correctly built, and that same test would only pass once the code was correctly built. Tests also ran automatically on TravisCI [16] when we pushed new code to GitHub, so it was easy to see whether a change caused a test to fail.

Checking against the best available data: the core step for making sure the simulation results are accurate was to compare them with real-world data that were not included when we built the model, whenever possible. This paper sums up the main checking steps that MICROSIM has gone through so far.

### How we judged the simulation evidence, and how the evidence is organized

MICROSIM is a Monte Carlo simulation that follows both people and the population. It uses different regression-based models to estimate the yearly chances of moving from one risk factor to another and from one outcome to another [12]. Regression-based models are statistical tools that estimate how one thing changes with others. Examples include logistic regression, which estimates the chance of a yes-or-no outcome, and Cox regression, which estimates how quickly an outcome changes over time. MICROSIM is designed so that data from common clinical and epidemiological sources can be applied directly to untangle the complicated ways that competing forces act on people, one at a time, in different groups. It also lets us understand population-level effects by adding up the results across people.

We based the model's assumptions and inputs on the best available evidence, and we designed them to fit directly with the best existing data sources and to be closely linked in their ideas. In particular, MICROSIM starts with people from population-level data that include each person's own features related to heart and blood vessel disease. It then models how risk factors and outcomes change over time using regression-based data from cohort studies. Finally, it can combine evidence from trials on treatment effects at the population level, so that the overall treatment effects match the trial evidence.

We chose the evidence using an evidence hierarchy, a ranking of how much weight to give each kind of evidence. We gave meta-analyses of randomized trials more weight than single randomized trials, and more weight than high-quality observational evidence. When none of these were available, we estimated effects using regression models. We used the BP COG pooled dataset, a combined dataset of results from 6 US studies that followed people forward in time and included each person's own data. These were the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study (ARIC) [17], Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults Study (CARDIA) [18], Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS) [19], Framingham Offspring Study (FOS) [20], Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), and Northern Manhattan Study (NOMAS) [21]. MICROSIM is designed to model scenarios for preventing heart and blood vessel disease and dementia based on earlier separate simulation models that estimated heart and blood vessel disease [2] and dementia prevention [22] (Fig 1).

In MICROSIM, we follow how healthy people (those without heart and blood vessel disease and dementia) move into other states. These include a non-ASCVD death, a fatal or non-fatal heart and blood vessel disease, all-cause dementia, or staying free of all of those events. MICROSIM updates the status of healthy people every year using Monte Carlo methods. The population is based on the nationally representative National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). We estimate the rates of moving from risk factors, from thinking and memory, to heart and blood vessel disease, to non-ASCVD death, and to all-cause dementia mainly with predictive models built from the BP COG pooled dataset. Treatment effects come directly from randomized controlled trials, as described in the "Simulation Details" sections below. Based on existing research, we give each person a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). This is a measure of how much of a healthy life a person lives, adjusted for how well they do.

### Simulation details

We describe MICROSIM's simulation details using the PARTE framework, which stands for Properties, Actions, Rules, Time, Environment. It was developed to describe the building blocks of agent-based models, which are computer models that follow individual people. MICROSIM should not be seen as an agent-based model, because people in the model do not directly affect one another. However, there is no widely accepted standard for reporting simulation models like MICROSIM, so we felt this framework matched the key parts of MICROSIM.

Simulation details: Properties [24]

In MICROSIM, each person is described by their starting features, mostly reflecting risk factors for clinical outcomes, and by clinical outcomes that build up over time. The starting features are: demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, less than high school, some high school, high school graduate, some college, college graduate); vascular risk factors (systolic and diastolic BP, or SBP and DBP, total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, glycosylated hemoglobin (HgbA1C)); biometrics (body mass index, or BMI, and waist circumference); behaviors relevant to vascular risk (physical activity, smoking); and medications (anti-hypertensive agents, statins, other lipid-lowering agents). The vascular risk factors are blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar. The triglycerides and LDL are fats in the blood, and the HDL is a good cholesterol. Glycosylated hemoglobin is a measure of blood sugar.

The population is made up of people. Clinical outcomes are all-cause dementia, thinking and memory, stroke, heart attack, death, and quality-adjusted life years (QALYS).

To build a population that represents the whole United States (US) population, and particular groups such as people with a particular condition, we start MICROSIM with NHANES data on adults 18 and older with no history of dementia, stroke, or heart attack. NHANES is a national survey that takes a snapshot of the health and nutrition of the US population, and it is repeated over time [25]. What makes it special is that it combines interviews with physical examinations. NHANES collects measurements of vascular risk factors using standard procedures.

In the combined NHANES dataset, we used multiple imputation with chained equations to fill in missing data. Imputation means estimating missing values from the information in the data. For each variable, we used all the other variables as covariates, which are factors that might affect the outcome. The exceptions were triglycerides and LDL, which were left out of models for each other because they were too closely linked to each other (collinearity), and anti-hypertensive medications, which were left out of the SBP and DBP models because of the same problem. For anti-hypertensive medications, we added an indicator variable for whether the patient's BP met the Eighth Joint National Committee (JNC-8) criteria for high blood pressure. We also added interactions between DBP, SBP, and JNC-8 hypertension status, and interactions between SBP, DBP, and self-reported hypertension, to make the model more predictive.

NHANES does not measure thinking and memory again and again, so we took the thinking and memory inputs from other sources. In earlier work, our group built models that follow people over time to predict overall thinking and memory using pooled and harmonized data from the six BP-COG cohorts (ARIC, CARDIA, CHS, FOS, MESA, NOMAS), which had repeated thinking and memory measurements [23, 26]. In short, trained staff gave participants the thinking and memory tests over time in person. We wanted to learn about thinking and memory as a whole, not about single test items, and to solve the problem of different tests being given to different cohorts. To do this, we combined the available test items into one factor, global cognitive performance (GCP), using item response theory methods and confirmatory factory analyses. Item response theory measures how well people do on a test. Confirmatory factory analyses use all the information in common across cohorts and test items unique to particular cohorts [27–30].

We estimated GCP scores with the regression-based method in Mplus, a statistics program. A 1-point difference in GCP means a 0.1 standard deviation difference in thinking and memory across the cohorts. A standard deviation is a measure of how spread out values are. Higher GCP scores mean better performance. At baseline, we gave each person an overall GCP level above or below average, drawn at random from the GCP random effect distribution. The random effect is a part of the model that lets each person's GCP differ from the average. We estimated each person's starting GCP by adding up the random effect with the fixed effects, which are the parts of the model that link GCP to the starting features.

Simulation details: Actions

In the current version of MICROSIM, people do not directly affect one another. Instead, the data at earlier time points are used to update each person's data at later time points, following the rules below. The exception is that treatment effects can be recalculated at the population level after all the individual effects have been updated, as needed to match the best available data, as described below.

Simulation details: Rules

Most changes in each person's data in MICROSIM come from regression models that predict the next value of a feature for that person at later time points. The rules are applied one after another: 1. Risk factors are updated, 2. Clinical outcomes are assigned based on the updated risk factors, 3. QALYS are assigned based on the clinical outcomes. The exception is that QALYS are assigned by a fixed set of rules.

Simulation details: Rules—change in risk factor levels over time [31]

We built regression models that follow people over time to predict each feature that changes over time in the starting population. These features were vascular risk factors, biometrics, vascular risk behaviors, and medications. We used pooled data from each person in the six BP-COG cohorts (ARIC, CARDIA, CHS, FOS, MESA, NOMAS). The predictors were race/ethnicity, smoking, gender, and the value of each feature at the immediately earlier time point, and the average value of each feature over all earlier time points. We also included all other features that change over time. We saved the regression results as JSON files, a common format for storing data, including the spread of the leftover variation in each person's results (the mean and standard deviation).

We moved forward one year at a time. For each person, we calculated the new level of each risk factor by adding up the values from the matching regression model, each multiplied by its coefficient (a number showing how strongly that feature is linked to the outcome), and then drawing a random value from the leftover variation. We took the logarithm of SBP and DBP values throughout, which makes the model fit better, and we took the original values back out when estimating the updated risk factor levels.

Simulation details: Rules—cardiovascular events

For each stage of the model, we calculated each person's risk of a heart and blood vessel event from their estimated vascular risk factor levels, using the updated pooled cohort equation (PCE). This equation predicts the risk of stroke, heart attack, or heart and blood vessel death [32]. We then gave each person an event, with a chance based on their yearly estimated risk.

Once we knew whether a person would have a heart and blood vessel event, we assigned the specific type of event using a separate model [33]. For people in the pooled BP-COG cohort with a stroke or heart attack, we built a logistic regression model that included factors known to predict stroke and heart attack differently. These were age, SBP, DBP, BMI, triglycerides, HgbA1C, gender, and race/ethnicity, using the values at the immediately earlier time point for all features that change over time. In the simulation, when a person had a heart and blood vessel event, we used the inverse logit of the stroke prediction model's values to find the chance that the event was a stroke. The inverse logit is a mathematical step that turns a model's prediction into a chance between 0 and 1. We then randomly sorted the events as stroke or heart attack using this chance. To decide whether a death from heart and blood vessel disease was fatal or not, we randomly assigned it as 0.15 for stroke [34–37] and 0.13 for heart attack [38].

Simulation details: Rules—death from non-cardiovascular causes [39]

After assigning heart and blood vessel events, we assigned deaths from non-cardiovascular causes using a similar approach. We estimated the risk of non-ASCVD death from a logistic regression model built in NHANES. We linked long-term death data to the combined NHANES dataset and identified the underlying causes of death. We then built a synthetic dataset. Each NHANES respondent-year was a row from the first NHANES response until the last follow-up date. A yes-or-no indicator showed whether the patient died from a non-ASCVD cause in that year.

We built a logistic regression model in this dataset to predict the time to non-ASCVD death. It took into account age, age squared (age multiplied by itself), race/ethnicity, gender, average SBP, average DBP, HgbA1C, total cholesterol, triglycerides, BMI, and smoking. We then estimated the chance of death in a given year by taking the logit of the model's values. We randomly assigned deaths using this chance. Otherwise, the patient stayed alive in the simulation until the next wave.

When we included this model in the full MICROSIM simulation, the population-level death rate was underestimated, especially in older adults. To correct for this, we recalibrated the age and age-squared coefficients, meaning we changed how strongly age is linked to the outcome. We did this by running a series of simulations in the full MICROSIM environment and changing the age and age-squared coefficients, and by measuring how far the population-level death rates strayed from US life tables. A life table is a standard table of death rates for a population. We kept the coefficients that gave the smallest squared deviation of age-specific predicted chances compared with US life tables.

Simulation details: Rules—thinking and memory and dementia

We estimated each person's future GCP from three things: their linear prediction from the GCP model (described above), their random effect, and a random draw from the overall leftover variation.

To sort dementia risk by risk factors, we built a Cox proportional hazards model to predict all-cause dementia. This model estimates how quickly an outcome changes over time. We used it for the BP-COG cohorts with data on new cases of dementia (ARIC, CHS, and FOS). CARDIA, MESA, and NOMAS did not have data on new cases of dementia. ARIC [17], CHS [40], and FOS [41] measured new cases of dementia by physician adjudication, which means doctors deciding who had dementia. They used standard diagnostic criteria, study-specific procedures, and all available data, including in-person neuropsychological and neurologic assessments, telephone interviews (participant or informant), brain imaging, and medical record review. The model predicting dementia included each person's baseline GCP scores, education, age, sex, race/ethnicity, and GCP slope (how GCP scores change over time). Table 1 summarizes these factors.

New cases of dementia are somewhat more common in the combined BP-COG cohorts (ARIC, CHS, FOS) than in an earlier meta-analysis of studies of how often dementia occurs, summarized in an equation by Brookmeyer et al. [42, 43]. This is likely because the two studies define dementia slightly differently. So we fitted a quadratic function, a curve that can bend, to the starting survival curve from the BP-COG cohort's Cox model. We then searched for changes in the curve's parameters that would make the final dementia incidence (new cases of dementia) most closely match the Brookmeyer equation. This recalibration can easily be "turned off" for a given analysis if the combined BP-COG incidence of dementia is thought to represent the incidence in the target population more accurately.

Simulation details: Rules—treatment effects

A central goal of this simulation is to estimate how heart and blood vessel events are affected in a counterfactual, where BP treatment differs from usual care. To do this, we need reliable estimates of how an extra anti-hypertensive medication affects risk.

MICROSIM uses effect size estimates, which are numbers that describe the size of an effect, taken directly from meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials or single randomized controlled trials when available. It works this out in two steps. First, it uses the effects from observational studies. Then it recalculates these effect sizes to match the effects seen in randomized controlled trials. In observational studies, the link between BP levels and heart and blood vessel events is generally weaker than the treatment effect seen in trials for anti-hypertensive medications [44]. In other words, an anti-hypertensive medication in a trial may lower BP by 5/3 mmHg and have a relative risk reduction (RR) of 0.2 for heart and blood vessel disease. The RR is the relative risk, which compares the risk of an event in the treated group with the risk in the untreated group. In observational data, people with BP 5/3 mmHg lower will have a smaller RR for heart and blood vessel disease, 0.1.

So we modeled the effects of anti-hypertensive treatment in two ways. First, we applied the average BP lowering seen across anti-hypertensive trials for each anti-hypertensive agent added, which is 5.5/3.1 mmHg [45]. In MICROSIM, BP treatments can be applied in one of two ways: they can be applied at a single point in time, or they can be applied again during each simulation wave. In both cases, the SBP and DBP in later waves will reflect the lower BP from the earlier wave. This lets us model different assumptions about how BP medicines affect the whole life course.

The default behavior is to apply a treatment at one point (for example, adding one medication to lower BP by 5.5/3.1 mmHg in a given wave) and then to have the lower BP in that wave predict the BP levels in later waves through the updating of risk factors. To make the treatment effects of heart and blood vessel disease match the randomized controlled trial evidence, we recalculated the treatment at the end of each year step. We adjusted for the smaller treatment effect of an extra anti-hypertensive medication on heart and blood vessel disease seen in trials, based on the trial/observational RR for each mm Hg BP reduction: 0.79 for stroke and 0.87 for heart attack. We did this by randomly rolling back heart and blood vessel events.

We randomly chose people who had received an extra anti-hypertensive medication to have their events rolled back. We weighted them by their inverse untreated risk, so the highest-risk patients would be the least likely to be chosen [29]. One strength of recalculating treatment effects at the population level is that it lets us add trial effects directly into the codebase, for example by adjusting the starting risk after a trial's relative risk reduction. This is not possible with more complex mathematical approaches that follow people forward in time. The main weakness of this approach is that it needs a lot of computing power. It also makes it harder to run the simulation in parallel, because each person can no longer be thought of as a separate Markov process.

Simulation details: Rules—Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYS)

We gave each person a QALY in each round of the simulation. If a person had no events (no heart attack, no stroke, and no dementia), we gave them an average QALY based on their age [46]. For events (stroke, heart attack, and all-cause dementia), we reduced each person's starting QALY by the relative effect of each age. For stroke and heart attack, the reduction varied. It was larger in the year of a new event (RR, 0.67 for stroke, RR, 0.88 for heart attack) and smaller in later years (RRs, 0.9 for both stroke and heart attack) [2]. For dementia, we used a multiplier of 0.80 for the first year of new dementia, with a 0.01 reduction in each later year. In other words, the multiplier was 0.75 for 5 years after dementia began [47].

Simulation details: Time [24]

In MICROSIM, time is measured in years. We start the simulation at a given year and match it to a starting NHANES wave. We then move forward one year and apply all the rules to each person. After all the people in a wave have been updated, we recalculated treatment effects at the population level, so that the treatment effects in the simulation match the effects measured in randomized trials. MICROSIM can move forward a fixed number of years. The default is to study the whole life course, moving forward until every person has died.

Simulation details: Environment

MICROSIM is designed to represent the US population. So each simulation run starts at a given year to represent the US population at a given point in time (1999–2017, including) [24], and a sample size. For a given starting year, we choose the matching NHANES wave to set the starting simulation features. We do this using survey-weighted sampling with replacement from the NHANES, at the chosen sample size. Survey-weighted sampling means each person's weight is adjusted for how likely they were to be picked in the survey. Sampling with replacement means a person can be picked more than once. Once the simulation is started, its starting environment does not change and does not interact with any people any further.

Simulation details: Summary of core assumptions

The central starting assumption of MICROSIM is that it reflects the US population at any given point in the 21st century. So the population, the starting levels of risk, and the unmeasured factors that cause risk factors and outcomes to change over time all reflect the average state of the US during this time. These assumptions are built into both the population-level data used to start the simulation and the data behind the risk and outcome models we chose for MICROSIM. A key implication of this assumption is that "usual care" means care that was actually delivered in the United States at a given time. This is central, but the MICROSIM framework lets us relax or change it by starting with a different set of population features and/or changing the risk factor and outcome models.

Several key assumptions about BP treatment are built into MICROSIM. We assume that BP treatment has narrow and specific effects. First, it lowers SBP and DBP by a standard average effect (5.5/3.1 mm Hg), and this level of BP reduction has a small effect in reducing the risk of heart and blood vessel events. Second, it lowers the risk of heart and blood vessel events further, so that the overall relative risk reduction of BP medicines matches the meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RR, 0.79 for stroke and RR, 0.87 for heart attack). Third, it improves GCP and lowers the risk of dementia only through the effect of lowering BP. So the effect of a BP-lowering medication on GCP comes entirely from lowering BP by 5/3 mm Hg, and the effect on dementia comes entirely from the effect on GCP.

Treatment effects work across the whole life course. When a BP treatment is applied, it lowers a simulated person's BP at a given point in time. When the person is "aged" forward, we use the treated BP to predict the BP in later waves through the updating of risk factors. So the effect of BP treatment over time may be larger or smaller over time, depending on the details of the risk factor updating models. This assumption can be changed within the existing MICROSIM treatment framework by specifying other BP treatment effects. For example, we could reduce BP in every wave on treatment by 5/3 mm Hg, without updating the risk factors in later waves. The default is to apply a BP treatment at one wave and then update BP through changes in risk factors over time [2, 17, 24, 32–47].

### Overview of the codebase

The simulation is organized around two core classes, Person and Population. The Person class mostly stores risk factors and outcomes, with properties and methods for getting and updating each person's state throughout the simulation. Time-varying properties are stored on Person objects as lists. Outcomes are stored as dictionaries, with a key for the clinical outcome and the value for the details of that outcome. The Population class manages a group of Persons. Each Population instance loads data from a given source, moves forward in time (one year), recalculates the population-level outcomes, and reports them simply.

To move forward, the Population uses Models. These calculate the next property (for example, a risk factor or outcome) for a Person, which comes from a Model Repository, a Model store that can also decide which Model to apply to a Person. Most Models are Regression Models, which take a series of regression coefficients and estimate each person's risk.

Each of these parts is designed to be adaptable and extensible to new populations, new parameters, and new risk models. For example, we could start the simulation with new data, and the Population class could then be subclassed, and that logic added to the started Person objects. In the same way, it is easy to change which Models are used to carry out the changes in particular factors over time. For example, we can easily swap the existing model of heart and blood vessel disease for a newer or different population risk model.

parts.title: Building and Testing MICROSIM: A Computer Model of How Long-Term Blood Pressure Control Affects Dementia and Heart Disease Across a Lifetime
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We urgently need ways to prevent or delay Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD), which are illnesses that slowly damage memory and thinking. Controlling blood pressure (BP) is a promising way to do this. Yet we do not know how different ways of controlling blood pressure, at different ages across a person's life, affect these diseases.

One way to find out would be a randomized trial, where people are split by chance into groups that get different treatments and are followed for many years. Such trials may not be possible here, because they would need to follow people for a very long time and would need a very large number of participants. A computer simulation is a practical way to estimate these effects using the best data we already have. However, existing simulation tools cannot estimate how blood pressure control affects both dementia and heart and blood vessel disease.

In this paper, we describe how we designed a new simulation tool, the MIchigan ChROnic Disease SIMulation (MICROSIM), how we built it, and how we checked it against real data for a whole population. We built it for a study called BP-COG (The Effect of Lower Blood Pressure over the Life Course on Late-life Cognition in Blacks, Hispanics, and Whites), which looks at how blood pressure levels across a lifetime affect dementia and heart and blood vessel disease.

MICROSIM is an agent-based Monte Carlo simulation. This means it follows many simulated people, each with their own health, and uses chance to decide what happens to each one, repeating the process many times. We wrote it following best practices in computer programming.

MICROSIM starts from a sample of US adults aged 18 and older that represents the whole country, based on the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). For each simulated person, it estimates their levels of risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease every year. It also estimates the chance that each person develops all-cause dementia, a stroke, a heart attack (myocardial infarction), or dies.

To model how risk factors change over time, and how thinking ability and dementia change, we used changes seen in a combined dataset of individual participants from 6 US studies that followed people forward over time to learn about heart and blood vessel disease. We estimated the risk of heart and blood vessel disease using a widely used risk model. We took the effects of blood pressure treatment from meta-analyses, which are studies that pool the results of many randomized trials.

MICROSIM is an extensible, open-source framework. This means others can add to it and freely use its code. It is designed to estimate how different ways of managing blood pressure affect a whole population. It reproduces US population-level estimates of blood pressure and other risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease, how these change over time, and how many people develop all-cause dementia, stroke, heart attack, or die.
parts.introduction_first:
Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) are major causes of death and disability in older people. Preventing or delaying these diseases can lead to longer lives, less disability, less time in nursing homes, lower health care costs, and a better quality of life.

Controlling blood pressure (BP) is a promising way to prevent or delay AD/ADRD. It is also the key part of preventing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), which is heart and blood vessel disease caused by fatty deposits building up in the arteries. This includes both preventing it in people who have not had it yet (primary prevention) and preventing it again in people who already have it (secondary prevention). The main examples are stroke and heart attack (acute myocardial infarction).

Still, little is known about how blood pressure treatment affects heart and blood vessel disease and AD/ADRD together, across a whole population.
parts.introduction_rest:
Over the past 20 years, more and more evidence has led to important new guidelines for doctors. These guidelines call for stronger treatment of risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease that people can change, such as blood pressure. Most of the studies and computer models that helped shape these guidelines, however, look only at how blood pressure affects heart and blood vessel disease. They do not look at how it affects AD/ADRD [1–4].

This matters because blood pressure is a strong risk factor for AD/ADRD. If we also consider how blood pressure affects AD/ADRD and other illnesses, doctors and policymakers may decide differently on what the "best" blood pressure treatment is.

Here is an example. Lowering blood pressure to the best level (below 120/80 mm Hg) reduces heart and blood vessel disease events, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and the combination of MCI and AD/ADRD in people who are at high risk of heart and blood vessel disease [5, 6]. MCI is a mild decline in thinking ability that is not yet dementia. But this group of people in the US is fairly small. We do not know whether lowering blood pressure to the best level also reduces heart and blood vessel disease and AD/ADRD in the much larger group of adults at lower risk of heart and blood vessel disease. One example is a Black person aged 55 whose systolic blood pressure (the top number) is 130–139 mmHg.

Suppose that treating blood pressure more strongly, starting early in life, has a large effect on thinking ability and AD/ADRD later in life. Then the best time to start treatment, the blood pressure level at which to start, and how strongly to treat should all shift toward younger ages and stronger treatment. In the same way, if we can estimate how strongly treating blood pressure affects heart and blood vessel disease separately from how it affects AD/ADRD, we may be able to describe more accurately how different blood pressure policies affect quality of life, cost-effectiveness (how much health benefit a policy gives for its cost), and benefit to society. That knowledge can help guide the best policy.

Large randomized trials are the least biased way to estimate how blood pressure treatment affects AD/ADRD, but such trials may not be possible. Right now, the most effective and practical way to estimate these effects may be computer simulations. These can draw on published risk models, on meta-analyses of randomized trials, and on the best available data from observational studies, which follow people in their everyday lives.

Some microsimulation models already exist for either heart and blood vessel disease or dementia. A microsimulation model follows many simulated people one by one. But no microsimulation model yet covers both heart and blood vessel disease and dementia.

In this paper, we describe how we designed a new population health microsimulation tool, MICROSIM, how we built it, and how we checked it against real data for a whole population. We built it for BP-COG (The Effect of Lower Blood Pressure over the Life Course on Late-life Cognition in Blacks, Hispanics, and Whites), a study of how blood pressure levels across a lifetime affect the decline in thinking ability and the development of dementia. We designed MICROSIM by following best practices in computer programming, to create a new simulation model of heart and blood vessel disease and AD/ADRD.

Our first research goal with this extensible, open-source framework is to explore a series of questions. We want to learn how different ways of managing blood pressure affect thinking ability later in life and all-cause dementia, and how they affect differences between races in how often all-cause dementia develops. Our ultimate research goal, though, is to build a framework that others can add to as new illnesses are included, so it can be used to answer many different questions about managing long-lasting diseases.

## How we checked the model, and what we found

### Our plan for checking the model

We wanted to find the parts of the model that would most likely affect how well it matches high-quality data that we had not used to build it. These parts matter for our main building blocks and our central research questions. For each of them, we chose the best way to check the model. The main parts we focused on were:

- whether the simulated population as a whole looks like the real US population;
- how levels of risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease change over time;
- how many people develop heart and blood vessel disease;
- how many people develop dementia.

### Checking the simulated population at the start [48]

Table 2 compares two simulated populations from MICROSIM with published figures from NHANES. The first is a simulated population of 500,000 people chosen at random. It matched the published figures for the 2007–2010 NHANES group almost exactly. That group was "survey-weighted", which means each person counted in proportion to how many people in the country they represent.

We also looked at people with high blood pressure (hypertension). We defined this as a systolic blood pressure (the top number, the pressure when the heart beats) above 140/90 mmHg, or taking medicine for high blood pressure. Our 500,000-person simulated group with hypertension matched a published survey-weighted NHANES group of people with hypertension in 2013 very well. This was true both for basic facts about who they were and for their levels of risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease.

### Checking how risk factors change over time in the simulated population [51]

The simulation closely reproduced how risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease changed over time in the real BP-COG groups (results not shown). But this check is somewhat circular, because we used those same groups to build the simulation's models. So we wanted a stronger test.

To do this, we compared a simulated group followed over time with a "pseudo-cohort" from NHANES. A pseudo-cohort is a group made by joining together people from separate NHANES surveys, each taken at a different point in time. We built a simulated population of 250,000 adults aged 18 or older that represents the whole country. None had a history of stroke, heart attack or dementia. We set it up using NHANES data from 1999 and then ran it forward for 18 years, until 2017, the most recent year with NHANES data. We then removed simulated people who died before 2017.

For the NHANES comparison, we included adults aged 36 or older. That is the age a person would be 18 years after the starting age of 18. We left out adults who had moved into the US, because the simulation does not include people moving in or out.

Fig 2 shows histograms, which are bar charts of how many people have each level of a risk factor. ### Checking how many people develop heart and blood vessel disease and die [52]

Table 3 sums up how many strokes and heart attacks MICROSIM estimated in a simulated population of 250,000 people from 1999 to 2015. We report these as "age-standardized" rates. This means the rates are adjusted so that differences in age between groups do not distort the comparison.

For heart attack, the simulation (set up in 1999) gave an average of 234 cases per 100,000 people each year. The 95% confidence interval was 232 to 241. A 95% confidence interval is a range that shows how precisely we know a value. MICROSIM's heart attack rate is broadly similar to the rate seen in the Kaiser Permanente health system, which ranged from 208 to 284 cases per 100,000 from 1999 to 2008 [53].

For stroke, the simulation gave an average of 153 cases per 100,000 people. This falls within the range reported in studies of whole populations over the same years, which ranged from 130 to 400 per 100,000 [54–56]. Hospitalization rates for stroke were around 200 per 100,000 [57].

### Checking the effects of treatment [59]

To see whether the simulation reproduced the real-world effects of blood pressure treatment, we ran 15 simulations. Each one followed a population of 150,000 people aged 18 and older, with no history of dementia, stroke or heart attack, for five years. The population was based on NHANES. We ran two versions.

In the first, the "as-treated" version, blood pressure treatment followed current practice, which we call usual care. In the second, every person added one blood pressure medicine to their current treatment. This lowered blood pressure by 5.5 mmHg on average for the top number and 3.1 mmHg for the bottom number.

We measured the effect as a relative risk. This compares the chance of an event in the treated group with the chance in the usual-care group. A value of 1 means no difference, and a value below 1 means fewer events. On average, the relative risk for stroke was 0.76, with a range of 0.72 to 0.82. For heart attack, it was 0.85, with a range of 0.81 to 0.89. These effects are close to the standard we used to set up the model. That standard came from a meta-analysis of trials that lowered blood pressure, which found a relative risk of 0.79 for stroke and 0.87 for heart attack [60].

### Checking how many people develop dementia [61]

Using NHANES, we created a population of 200,000 people aged 18 and older that represents the whole country. None had a history of dementia, stroke or heart attack. We ran the simulation for 20 years and estimated how many people developed all-cause dementia.

Fig 4 compares the all-cause dementia rate from MICROSIM with the age-by-age dementia curve from a meta-analysis by Brookmeyer and colleagues [42]. The two matched closely across all ages.

### Showing how a model that follows both individuals and the whole population could be useful

One possible strength of MICROSIM is that it follows both individuals and the whole population. This lets it estimate different quantities within one framework, even though each would usually need a different kind of study.

For example, a common method called a fixed probability decision analysis estimates the average effect across a whole population. It asks questions such as: for a given blood pressure treatment plan, how many quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) are gained compared with usual care? A QALY is a year of life lived in good health, where a year in poor health counts for less than a full year. In a similar way, regression analysis of cohort studies can estimate how much results differ between groups and within groups for different blood pressure treatment plans. Regression is a statistical method for measuring how an outcome changes with different factors. MICROSIM's design lets us estimate both kinds of quantities, and how they affect each other.

To show how this combined approach can describe effects on the whole population, on individuals, and in groups defined by factors we care about, we ran a simple model. It compared two groups of 300,000 people aged 18 or older. All had high blood pressure at the start and no history of dementia, stroke or heart attack. In the first group, they got usual care. In the second, they got intensive blood pressure control, based on the Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT) [5].

MICROSIM estimated a small gain in average QALYs for the whole population with intensive blood pressure control compared with usual care: 20.9 versus 20.8. This is similar to the kind of result a fixed probability decision analysis would give.

However, we also found that the average gain in QALYs for each person varied across the population (Fig 5). We split people into four equal-sized groups, called quartiles, by their starting blood pressure. People in the lowest quarter had no difference in QALYs (32.2 versus 32.2 QALYs). People in the highest quarter had a much larger gain (13.7 versus 13.4 QALYs).

Fig 6 shows how QALYs were spread out within each of these four groups. The small differences in average QALYs between groups make up only a very small part of the overall spread in QALYs from person to person. This is similar to the kind of result a regression analysis of a cohort study would give.
