## Discussion

In this paper, we describe how we built a new computer simulation that follows many simulated people over time to study heart and blood vessel disease and dementia. We call it MICROSIM. It is open-source, so anyone can use and change its code, and it is extensible, so others can add to it. It starts from a sample of people that represents a whole population. We first designed it to explore how different ways of treating blood pressure affect heart and blood vessel disease and thinking ability. The main parts of the simulation that we needed for those goals match well with what is known about whole populations. We also built it so that it is fairly easy to change, for example by swapping in a different risk model for one disease. It is also easy to extend, either to add new health outcomes or to add more detail about how diseases develop and are treated.

In its current form, MICROSIM has everything it needs to answer a set of research questions about risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease, how those risk factors are managed, heart and blood vessel disease, dementia, and quality of life. It is also fairly easy to make small changes to this basic framework to answer many related questions. For example, we could use it to project future heart and blood vessel disease and dementia under different assumptions about risk, or with different definitions of what counts as each disease. We could also use it to judge whether blood pressure treatment is worth its cost, either counting the value of thinking ability or not.

Perhaps even more important, because the framework can be extended, it opens the door to including many more things. These include other diseases, such as congestive heart failure (when the heart cannot pump enough blood to the body), peripheral vascular disease (poor blood flow to the legs and arms), and chronic kidney disease. They also include risk markers, such as social determinants of health, meaning the social and economic conditions in which people live. Other examples are treatments, such as statins (medicines that lower cholesterol) and oral hypoglycemics (medicines that lower blood sugar), and public health measures, such as access to healthy food and green spaces. With these additions, the simulation could answer a huge range of research questions.

In ongoing work, we are also building ways to easily simulate clinical trials and to add more detailed information about the features of each disease. In particular, we are expanding the simulation to study how risk factors are managed after a stroke. To do this, we are including the type of stroke, the different kinds of ischemic stroke (a stroke caused by a blockage in the blood vessels), and how severe the stroke is.

We believe MICROSIM's main strengths are three. First, we built it following the best principles of software design. Second, we used the best data available to work out the main assumptions the simulation rests on. Third, we checked its main parts against real data from outside the studies we built it from. As far as we know, following programming best practices is fairly unusual for a simulation built by researchers. We believe this will give us code that is reliable enough to draw accurate conclusions about whole populations.

MICROSIM's main limitations are that, like any simulation, its results are only as strong as the main assumptions it rests on. Because it is complex, it relies on many assumptions that are hard to check directly with the evidence we have today. One example is how blood pressure treatment affects thinking ability. As stronger evidence comes out, we intend to keep updating MICROSIM with the best evidence available.

In the same way, the model assumes that relationships are fairly simple, when in reality they may be more complicated. One example is the possible J-shaped curve linking diastolic blood pressure (the lower number in a blood pressure reading) to the risk of death. In this pattern, the risk of death is lowest at a middle level of diastolic blood pressure and rises again at both lower and higher levels. So, to use MICROSIM well for a particular research question, researchers will need to think about how its assumptions might affect the results. When an uncertain assumption could plausibly change the conclusions, researchers could run robust sensitivity analyses. These are checks in which they change that assumption and see whether the results change.

Finally, we included race in the regression models that MICROSIM is built on. Regression models are statistical tools that estimate how a health outcome depends on several factors at once. However, the data we used to build these models were often not enough to capture the effects of Hispanic ethnicity, for example on dementia. Hispanic people are included in the model, but it is not clear that MICROSIM would reproduce estimates of outcomes for Hispanic people at the level of the whole society.

## Methods

### What we set out to learn, and the questions that drove us

We built MICROSIM following best practices in systems science, the study of how many parts of a system affect one another [7]. Our main goal was to use data from the past to learn how controlling blood pressure across a whole population, at different ages across a lifetime, would affect three things: heart and blood vessel disease, dementia, and the racial gap in both. Existing population simulations touch on parts of these questions. As far as we know, though, no simulation has tackled all of them at once, or could account for the trade-offs between heart and blood vessel disease and dementia.

Several specific questions shaped how we designed MICROSIM. First, better blood pressure control means less decline in thinking ability and a lower risk of dementia at any given age. It also means longer life, because people avoid heart and blood vessel events. But age is the biggest risk factor for both dementia and death from other causes. So how do these effects balance out? Does blood pressure treatment lower the risk of dementia across a person's whole life, or mostly push it later?

Second, blood pressure treatment has a large effect on the risk of dementia. Does that translate into a meaningful number of extra years lived without dementia?

Third, how do these patterns differ by race? Black people develop dementia more often than white people, but they also have more strokes. So if stronger blood pressure control helps Black people live longer by preventing strokes, could the racial gap in dementia actually grow?

Alongside these questions about whole populations, we also wanted to describe how these results vary from person to person. For example, how does the benefit differ for people with different starting risks of heart and blood vessel disease and of dementia, and for people living different lives?

Our first design of MICROSIM was built around these questions. We also designed it to be as open as possible, to make the code as accurate as possible, and to make it easy to extend for many other questions about managing long-term diseases.

### Why we chose a simulation

Randomized trials are the best way to find out how well different ways of treating blood pressure work on thinking ability and heart health together. These include how strongly blood pressure is lowered, when treatment starts, and which patients are chosen for it. But such trials are hard to design for these questions.

Ideally, we would want evidence from large, long randomized trials about how blood pressure, and blood pressure treatment, across a lifetime affect thinking ability and dementia in older age. Such trials would be at best awkward and expensive, and at worst impossible. They would need enormous numbers of people, careful tracking of every case, and strict control of the treatment, all kept up for decades. They would also be hard to carry out, and meaningful results would probably take decades. By then, the way doctors treat blood pressure may have changed so much that the results would no longer be useful. Even if these problems could be solved, such studies would not help patient care in the near term.

Shorter trials are easier, but they cannot directly show how short-term treatment choices affect long-term results. To do that, researchers would have to assume how much short-term stand-in measures matter, or stretch results from people at higher risk to people at lower risk.

Simulations follow how the key trade-offs for each person change over time. So they may be able to guide decisions when clinical trials are not possible, and give early guidance on important medical questions while we wait for better, long-term trials. Simulations can also combine the strengths of the best available data. First, they can use the best available data from studies that follow people over time. This lets them capture the complicated natural history of diseases and competing risks, where one event can prevent another from happening. Second, they can use the best estimates of how well treatments work: results from trials when they exist, and the best estimates from observational studies [8] when they do not. This lets them credibly cover a range of possible treatment effects. Used in a carefully set-up framework, simulations may be the best tools for estimating long-term treatment effects, especially in people at low risk. Simulations can also act as "policy laboratories." They let us explore what medical and policy choices would mean for society, and how much each policy would likely achieve compared with others.

Simulations also have several weaknesses. Because they are so complex, they can seem like "black box science," where the inner workings are hidden. This often leads to a lack of openness and to doubts about whether the results are accurate. Also, most current models are built separately and do not build on one another. This limits progress and may add to concerns about accuracy. Building a framework for a good simulation can be complicated and take a lot of time, and it requires carefully weighing many individual decisions. For the agent-based simulation we describe here, thinking carefully about the model's inputs is critical.

We built one simulation that answers several scientific questions at once, for both individuals and whole populations. Our reasoning is that a single codebase, shared across many questions, is more efficient and likely to give more reliable results than several simulations built for separate questions. This design has three specific advantages.

First, it lets us fairly easily measure effects for both individuals and whole populations, in fine detail. Suppose we want to know how blood pressure treatment affects a population. A Markov simulation, which moves each person from one health state to the next based on the chance of each move, would suit that task well, using population-level settings as inputs. If we also wanted to know how results vary between individuals, for example how the effect of treatment depends on a person's starting blood pressure, we could change that model to track results across different starting blood pressures. But extending it to other individual effects, such as how treatment depends on age, starting cholesterol, blood sugar, or other treatments, would take a lot of work. Our approach estimates many kinds of individual and population effects without changing the core simulation code. It does this by keeping track, roughly, of how various risk factors tend to rise and fall together.

Second, the code can be reused and easily changed to answer a wide range of questions. Besides measuring how blood pressure treatment affects racial differences in thinking ability and dementia in older age, for both individuals and populations, our project has a second goal: to explore possible designs for clinical trials on these questions. We can reuse the main MICROSIM codebase directly to test trial designs. In a MICROSIM subpackage [9], we built a simple codebase that describes trials and trial groups, runs simulated trials within MICROSIM, and pulls out the MICROSIM data for analysis. For example, we can run simulated trials of different ways of lowering blood pressure in different groups of people, chosen by their starting risk of heart and blood vessel disease and of dementia. This shows which groups make the most efficient trials. In the same way, we can explore how the features of a trial's population, such as its size and starting risks, combine with how long the trial lasts, given that the risk of dementia does not rise in a straight line at older ages.

Third, the simulation's inputs match existing population health data and ideas well. The aim behind our questions is to estimate how each person changes over time, then add up the individual results to get the population result. This is the same basic idea behind cohort studies, which follow groups of people over time. The main downside is that this approach needs much more coding and computing time than simpler models. In this paper, we describe how we built our simulation of heart and blood vessel disease and dementia for individuals and populations, and how we tried to reduce some of the general weaknesses of simulations.

### Principles for designing the simulation

To run a simulation, we write computer code that holds the simulation's logic and the chance-based parts that create the data. These codebases are often large, with tens of thousands of lines of code or more. The bigger the code, the more bugs we expect [10]. To make sure a simulation gives accurate and reliable results, we need good software development habits, so that the code carries out the simulation's logic with good quality. With this in mind, we developed a set of principles and strategies, based on best practices in computer programming, to guide how we built MICROSIM: Transparency, Readability, Simplicity, Testing, and Validation [11]. We hope that building a simulation on these principles will make it more reliable and accurate. We also hope that a framework that can be extended to many problems about managing long-term diseases will let other researchers build on it, making later analyses as reliable and valid as possible.

Transparency: simply knowing that other groups might look at your code encourages writers to program carefully and make sure the code is readable and makes sense. The entire MICROSIM codebase [12] is freely available on GitHub [12]. This includes the notebooks we used to build MICROSIM's inputs and the notebooks we used for the validation analyses [13] in this paper. Opening the code to other researchers also widens the group of people who use it. That makes it more likely that someone will spot errors in the simulation, and it makes the simulation more rigorous and easier to repeat.

Readability: the easier the code is to read, the less likely errors are to creep in. We used three main strategies. First, we hired a software developer with industry experience (coauthor LC, Ann Arbor, MI) to help with the coding and the software development methods. Second, we built the core parts of the simulation through pair programming, where two coders (JB and LC) sat side by side and shared one keyboard to write the key parts together. Third, we used an automatic formatting tool (Black [14]) that ran every time a file was saved. This kept the code style consistent and predictable, making it easier to read and write.

Simplicity: whenever possible, we used the simplest possible model structures and assumptions. The simpler the logic, the less likely it is to be put into code with an error. We meant this principle to apply both to the code and to the overall structure of the simulation. At the code level, it is mostly about priorities. If a fairly simple way of storing data can hold the data, it should be chosen over a more complex one. In the same way, more complex statistical models may describe the data slightly better, but unless they bring major gains in performance, simpler models should be chosen, because they are less likely to be put into code with an error.

Testing: in a large codebase, a change in one part may have unintended effects somewhere else. To reduce this risk, we used unit tests, which are small tests that check one piece of code at a time. We mostly used a "test-driven" approach [15]: for a new piece of code or a bug fix, we first wrote a test that would fail until the code was done correctly, and that same test would only pass once the code was done correctly. The tests also ran automatically on TravisCI [16], a service that runs tests whenever new code is pushed to GitHub. This made it easy to see if a change had broken a test.

Validation against the best available data: the most important step in making sure the simulation's results are accurate was to compare them, whenever possible, with real-world data that were not used to build the model. This paper summarizes the main validation steps MICROSIM has gone through so far.

### How we chose and organized the evidence for the simulation

MICROSIM is a Monte Carlo simulation for both populations and individuals. It uses different regression-based models, which are statistical tools that estimate how an outcome depends on several factors. For example, it uses logistic regression for yes-or-no outcomes, such as whether a person has an event, and Cox regression for time-to-event data, such as how long until a person has an event. With these models, it estimates the chance each year that a person moves from one risk factor or health state to another [12]. MICROSIM is designed so that data from common medical and population health sources can be applied directly. This lets it untangle the complicated ways that competing forces interact for each individual, across people who differ from one another, and then understand population-level effects by adding up the results across individuals.

We based the model's assumptions and inputs on the best available evidence. We also designed them to fit directly with, and be closely linked in idea to, the best existing data sources. In particular, MICROSIM starts with individuals from population-level data that include each person's physical traits related to heart and blood vessel disease. It then models how risk factors and health outcomes change over time, using regression-based data from cohort studies. Finally, evidence from trials on treatment effects can be added at the population level, so that the overall treatment effects match what trials found.

We chose the evidence using an evidence hierarchy, a ranking of sources. It put meta-analyses of randomized trials first, then individual randomized trials, then high-quality observational evidence. When none of these were available, we estimated effects using regression models. For these, we used the BP-COG pooled dataset, which combines individual participant data from six well-described US studies that followed people forward over time to learn about heart and blood vessel disease: the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study (ARIC) [17], the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults Study (CARDIA) [18], the Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS) [19], the Framingham Offspring Study (FOS) [20], the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), and the Northern Manhattan Study (NOMAS) [21]. MICROSIM is designed to model ways of preventing heart and blood vessel disease and dementia, based on earlier, separate simulation models for preventing heart and blood vessel disease [2] and preventing dementia [22] (Fig 1).

In MICROSIM, we look at how healthy people, meaning people free of heart and blood vessel disease and of dementia, move into one of four states: death from other causes, heart and blood vessel disease that is fatal or not fatal, all-cause dementia, or staying free of all of these events. MICROSIM updates the state of healthy people every year using Monte Carlo methods. The simulated population comes from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), which represents the whole US. The levels of risk factors, thinking ability, heart and blood vessel events, death from other causes, and all-cause dementia are estimated mainly from predictive models built from the BP-COG pooled cohort dataset. Treatment effects come directly from randomized trials, as described in the "Simulation details" sections below. Based on existing research, each state is given a number of quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), a measure that counts years of life while also taking into account how good that life is.

### Simulation details

We describe how MICROSIM works using the PARTE framework (Properties, Actions, Rules, Time, Environment), which was developed to describe the building blocks of agent-based models. MICROSIM is not an agent-based model, because individuals in it do not interact directly with one another. However, since there is no widely accepted standard for reporting simulation models like MICROSIM, we felt this framework matched the key parts of MICROSIM.

#### Simulation details: Properties [24]

Each person in MICROSIM has starting properties, mostly risk factors for health outcomes, and health outcomes that build up over time. The starting properties are:

- demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, and education: less than high school, some high school, high school graduate, some college, college graduate);
- vascular risk factors (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, the top and bottom numbers of a blood pressure reading; total cholesterol; triglycerides; low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol; high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol; and glycosylated hemoglobin (HgbA1C), a measure of average blood sugar over the past few months);
- body measurements (body mass index (BMI), a measure of weight relative to height, and waist size);
- behaviors that affect vascular risk (physical activity and smoking);
- medicines (blood pressure medicines, statins, and other medicines that lower cholesterol);
- vascular events before the simulation began (stroke, heart attack, and thinking ability).

Populations are described by adding up the results for all the individuals. The health outcomes are all-cause dementia, thinking ability, stroke, heart attack, death, and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs).

To build a population that represents the whole US, and also specific groups (for example, people with a particular condition), MICROSIM starts with data on adults aged 18 and older with no history of dementia, stroke, or heart attack from NHANES. NHANES is a survey that represents the whole country and is repeated over time, designed to measure the health and nutrition of the US population [25]. What makes it unusual is that it combines interviews with physical examinations. NHANES measures vascular risk factors using standard methods.

Some values in the combined NHANES dataset were missing. To fill these gaps, we used a method called multiple imputation with chained equations. It estimates each missing value from the other information available, and it repeats this many times to show how uncertain the estimate is. For each missing value, the method used all the other values as predictors, with a few exceptions. Triglycerides and LDL were left out of each other's models because they tend to rise and fall together (collinearity). Blood pressure medicines were left out of the models for systolic and diastolic blood pressure for the same reason. To make the estimates of blood pressure medicines more accurate, the models also added three things: a marker of whether a person's blood pressure counted as high under the Eighth Joint National Committee (JNC-8) criteria; interactions between diastolic blood pressure, systolic blood pressure, and JNC-8 high blood pressure status; and interactions between systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and whether the person said they had high blood pressure. An interaction lets the effect of one factor depend on the level of another.

NHANES does not measure thinking ability again and again over time, so we took the inputs for the thinking ability model from other sources. In earlier work, our group built models that predict overall thinking ability (global cognitive performance, or GCP) over time. These used pooled and harmonized data, meaning data combined and put on the same scale, from the six BP-COG cohorts (ARIC, CARDIA, CHS, FOS, MESA, NOMAS) that measured thinking ability repeatedly [23, 26]. In short, trained staff from each cohort gave participants thinking ability tests in person, again and again over time.

The cohorts used different thinking ability tests, and we wanted to study broad areas of thinking rather than single test questions. So we combined the available test questions into one score for overall thinking ability, using item response theory and confirmatory factor analyses [27–30]. These are statistical methods that combine many related measurements into a single underlying score. They use all the thinking ability information shared across cohorts, as well as questions found only in particular cohorts. We estimated the overall thinking ability scores with a regression-based method in the software Mplus. In this method, a 1-point difference means a 0.1 standard deviation difference in thinking ability across the cohorts (a standard deviation is a measure of how spread out values are). Higher scores mean better performance. At the start, each person was given an overall thinking ability level above or below average. This was a random draw from the part of the score that varies between people (the random effect), added to the part that is predicted from their starting characteristics (the fixed effects).

#### Simulation details: Actions

In the current version of MICROSIM, individuals do not interact directly with one another. Instead, each person's data at earlier times are used to estimate their data at later times, following the rules below. The one exception is that treatment effects can be recalibrated at the population level, after all the individual effects have been updated as needed to match the best available data, as described below.

#### Simulation details: Rules

Most changes for each person in MICROSIM come from regression models that predict a person's next value for a property at the next time point. The rules are applied in order: 1. Risk factors are updated. 2. Health outcomes are assigned based on the updated risk factors. 3. QALYs are assigned based on the health outcomes. The exception is the assignment of QALYs, which is done by a fixed set of steps.

#### Simulation details: Rules—change in risk factor levels over time [31]

We built regression models that follow people over time to predict each person's level of each factor that changes over time in the starting population. These factors were vascular risk factors, body measurements, vascular risk behaviors, and medicines. The thing being predicted was each factor's level, and the predictors were pooled individual participant data from the six BP-COG cohorts (ARIC, CARDIA, CHS, FOS, MESA, NOMAS). The predictors were race/ethnicity, smoking, gender, the factor's level at the immediately previous time point, the average of the factor's levels across all earlier time points, and all the other factors that change over time.

We saved the regression results as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) files, which include the mean and standard deviation of the residuals. Residuals are the leftover differences between what a model predicts and what actually happened. Moving forward one year at a time, we calculated each person's new level of each risk factor by adding a random draw from the residual distributions to the linear predictor. The linear predictor is the sum of all the regression coefficients multiplied by the person's values for each factor. Throughout, we used the logarithm of systolic and diastolic blood pressure values to help the models fit better, and converted them back when estimating each person's updated risk factor levels.

#### Simulation details: Rules—heart and blood vessel events

At each stage of the model, we calculated a person's risk of a heart and blood vessel event from their estimated vascular risk factor levels. We used the updated Pooled Cohort Equation (PCE), a widely used risk model that predicts the risk of stroke, heart attack, or death from heart and blood vessel disease [32]. To assign events, each person was given an event with a probability based on their estimated risk for that year.

After deciding whether a person would have a heart and blood vessel event, we used a separate model to decide which type of event it was [33]. Using people with a stroke or heart attack in the pooled BP-COG cohort, we built a logistic regression model. It included factors known to predict stroke and heart attack differently: age, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, BMI, triglycerides, HgbA1C, gender, and race/ethnicity. For all factors that change over time, we used their values from the previous time point. In the simulation, when a person was given a heart and blood vessel event, we used the inverse logit of the linear predictor from the stroke prediction model to get the probability that the event was a stroke. The inverse logit turns a model's output into a probability between 0 and 1. We then randomly classified the event as a stroke or a heart attack using this probability. Whether a heart and blood vessel event was fatal was decided by randomly assigning death, with a chance of 0.15 for stroke [34–37] and 0.13 for heart attack [38].

#### Simulation details: Rules—death from other (non-heart) causes [39]

After assigning heart and blood vessel events, we assigned death from other causes in a similar way. We estimated the risk of death from other causes with a logistic regression model built from NHANES data. To build it, we linked long-term death records to the combined NHANES dataset and identified the underlying cause of each death. We then built a made-up dataset in which each NHANES person-year became one row, running from the first NHANES response until the last follow-up date. A yes-or-no marker showed whether the person died from a non-heart cause in that year.

In this dataset, we built a logistic regression model that predicted the time to death from other causes, after taking into account age, age squared, race/ethnicity, gender, average systolic blood pressure, average diastolic blood pressure, HgbA1C, total cholesterol, triglycerides, BMI, and smoking. We then estimated the probability of death in a given year by taking the logit of the linear predictor from this model. We randomly assigned death using this probability. If the person did not die, they stayed alive in the simulation and moved on to the next year.

When we added this model to the full MICROSIM simulation, it underestimated deaths in the population, especially in older adults. To fix this, we recalibrated the age and age-squared coefficients. We ran repeated simulations in the full MICROSIM environment, changed the age and age-squared coefficients, and measured how far the population's deaths strayed from US life tables, which are standard tables of how many people die at each age. We kept the coefficients that gave the smallest squared difference between the predicted chances of death at each age and the US life tables.

#### Simulation details: Rules—thinking ability and dementia

We estimated each person's future overall thinking ability scores from three things: the person's linear predictor from the thinking ability model (described above), the person's random effect, and a random draw from the overall residual distribution.

To spread dementia risk across different risk factors, we built a Cox proportional hazards model to predict all-cause dementia. This model uses the BP-COG cohorts that had data on new cases of dementia (ARIC, CHS, and FOS). CARDIA, MESA, and NOMAS did not have data on new cases of dementia. In ARIC [17], CHS [40], and FOS [41], new cases of dementia were decided by doctors using standard diagnostic criteria, each study's own methods, and all available data. This included in-person thinking and neurologic tests, telephone interviews (with the participant or someone who knew them), brain imaging, and medical record reviews. The model included each person's starting overall thinking ability score, education, age, sex, race/ethnicity, and the slope of their thinking ability score (how much it changed over time). New cases of dementia are somewhat more common in the combined BP-COG cohorts (ARIC, CHS, FOS) than in an earlier meta-analysis of population studies of dementia, summarized in an equation by Brookmeyer and colleagues [42, 43]. This is likely because the studies define dementia slightly differently. So we fitted a quadratic function, a smooth curve, to the starting survival curve from the BP-COG Cox model. We then searched through possible values for the curve's settings to find the ones that made the final rate of new dementia cases match the Brookmeyer equation most closely. This recalibration can easily be "turned off" for a given analysis, if the combined BP-COG cohorts are thought to represent the rate of new dementia cases in the target population more accurately.

#### Simulation details: Rules—treatment effects

A central goal of this simulation is to estimate how heart and blood vessel events would change if blood pressure treatment were different from usual care. To do this, we need reliable estimates of how adding one more blood pressure medicine affects risk.

Whenever possible, MICROSIM uses effect sizes taken directly from meta-analyses of randomized trials or from individual randomized trials. In practice, it first applies effects from observational studies and then recalibrates these effect sizes to match what trials found. In observational studies, the link between blood pressure levels and heart and blood vessel events usually underestimates how much blood pressure medicines lower the risk in trials [44]. In other words, it underestimates the relative risk reduction (RRR), which is how much the risk drops compared with people who are not treated. In a trial, a blood pressure medicine may lower blood pressure by 5/3 mmHg and have a relative risk reduction for heart and blood vessel disease of 0.2. In observational data, people whose blood pressure is 5/3 mmHg lower have a smaller relative risk reduction, 0.1.

So we modeled the effects of blood pressure medicines in two steps. First, we applied the average blood pressure lowering seen across trials for each medicine added, which is 5.5/3.1 mmHg [45]. In MICROSIM, blood pressure treatment can be applied in one of two ways: once at a single point in time, or again in every simulation year. In both cases, systolic and diastolic blood pressure in later years reflect the lower blood pressure from the earlier year. This lets us model different ideas about how blood pressure medicines affect people over their lives. The default is to apply a treatment at one point in time (for example, add one medicine to lower blood pressure by 5.5/3.1 mmHg in a given year), and then let the lower blood pressure in that year predict later blood pressure levels through the risk factor updates.

To make the effects of treatment on heart and blood vessel disease match the trial evidence, we added a treatment recalibration step at the end of each year. It adjusted for the smaller effect of an extra blood pressure medicine on heart and blood vessel disease seen in trials, based on the trial and observational relative risk reduction for each mmHg of blood pressure lowered. The relative risk (RR) is the risk with treatment divided by the risk without it. We used a relative risk of 0.79 per blood pressure medicine for stroke and 0.87 per blood pressure medicine for heart attack, and we randomly rolled back heart and blood vessel events. People who received an extra blood pressure medicine were randomly chosen to have their events rolled back. The chance of being chosen depended on their risk without treatment, in inverse proportion, so that the highest-risk patients were the least likely to be chosen [29].

One strength of applying treatment effects by recalibrating at the population level is that it lets us add trial effects directly into the code. For example, we can adjust a person's starting risk afterward by the relative risk reduction estimated in a trial. This is simpler than adding these effects through more complex mathematical approaches that look ahead. The main weakness is that this approach takes a lot of computing power. It also makes it harder to run the simulation in parallel, because each person can no longer be thought of as a separate Markov process.

#### Simulation details: Rules—Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs)

We assigned QALYs to each person in every run. If a person had no events (no heart attack, stroke, or dementia), they were given an average QALY based on their age [46]. For events (stroke, heart attack, and all-cause dementia), the starting age-based QALY was reduced by a relative amount for each age. For stroke and heart attack, the size of the reduction was larger in the year the event happened (relative risk of 0.67 for stroke and 0.88 for heart attack) and smaller in later years (relative risk of 0.9 for both) [2]. For dementia, we used a multiplier of 0.80 in the first year of new dementia, with a 0.01 reduction in each later year. (So 5 years after dementia, the multiplier is 0.75) [47].

#### Simulation details: Time [24]

Time in MICROSIM is measured in years. The simulation starts in a given year, matched to a starting NHANES survey round. It then moves forward one year, and all the rules are applied to each person. After all people have been updated in a given year, the population-level recalibration for treatment effects is applied, so that the treatment effects in the simulation match those measured in randomized trials. MICROSIM can be moved forward by a fixed number of years, but the default is to study the whole life course, moving the population forward until every person has died.

#### Simulation details: Environment

MICROSIM is designed to represent the US population. So each run starts with a starting year, which represents the US population at a given point in time (1999–2017, including) [24], and a sample size. For a given starting year, the matching NHANES survey round is chosen to set each person's starting properties. The starting sample is drawn from NHANES using survey weights, which give each person a weight that makes the sample represent the whole country, and with replacement, meaning the same person can be picked more than once. Once the simulation has started, the starting environment does not change and does not interact with the individuals any further.

#### Simulation details: Summary of core assumptions

The central starting assumption of MICROSIM is that it reflects the US population at any given point in the 21st century. So the population, the starting levels of risk, and the unmeasured factors that drive changes in risk factors and health outcomes over time all reflect the average situation in the US during this period. These assumptions are built into both the population-level data used to start the simulation and the data behind the risk and outcome models chosen for MICROSIM. A key result of this assumption is that "usual care" means the care that was actually given in the United States at a given time. Although this assumption is central, the MICROSIM framework lets it be loosened or changed, either by starting with a different set of population settings, by changing the risk factor and outcome models, or both.

MICROSIM also builds in several key assumptions about blood pressure treatment. Blood pressure treatment is assumed to have narrow, specific effects: 1. It lowers systolic and diastolic blood pressure by a standard average amount (5.5/3.1 mmHg), and this level of lowering has a small effect in reducing the risk of heart and blood vessel events. 2. It further lowers the risk of heart and blood vessel events, so that the overall relative risk reduction of blood pressure medicines matches meta-analyses of trials (relative risk of 0.79 per blood pressure medicine for stroke and 0.87 per blood pressure medicine for heart attack). 3. It improves overall thinking ability and lowers the risk of dementia, but only through its effect of lowering blood pressure. So the effect of a blood pressure medicine on thinking ability comes entirely from lowering blood pressure by 5/3 mmHg, and its effect on dementia comes entirely from the effect on thinking ability.

Treatment effects work across a person's whole life. When a blood pressure treatment is applied, it lowers a simulated person's blood pressure at a given point in time. When the person is "aged" forward, the treated blood pressure is used to predict their later blood pressure through the risk factor updates. So the effect of blood pressure treatment over time may grow larger or smaller, depending on the details of the risk factor update models. This assumption can be changed within MICROSIM's existing treatment framework by setting other blood pressure treatment effects (for example, lowering blood pressure by 5/3 mmHg in every year of treatment, without updating later risk factors). But the default is to apply a blood pressure treatment in one year and then let later blood pressure be updated through changes in the risk factor models over time [2, 17, 24, 32–47].

### Overview of the code

The simulation is built around two core classes, Person and Population. A class is a template for a type of object in the code. The Person class mainly stores a person's risk factors and health outcomes, with methods to get and update the person's state throughout the simulation. Properties that change over time are stored on each Person object as lists. Outcomes are stored as dictionaries, with a key for the health outcome that happened and a value for the details of that outcome. The Population class manages a group of People. Each Population instance loads data from a given data source, moves the population forward in time (one year at a time), recalibrates population-level outcomes, and does simple reporting. To help move the population forward, the Population uses Models. These calculate a person's next property (for example, a risk factor or an outcome). The Models are kept in a Model Repository, a store that can also decide which Model to apply to a person. Most Models are Regression Models, which take a set of regression coefficients and estimate the risk for a given person.

Each of these parts is designed to be adaptable and easy to extend with new populations, new settings, and new risk models. For example, one could start the simulation with new data, and the Population class could then be subclassed (a new version of the class), with that logic added to the Person objects at the start. In the same way, it is easy to change which Models are used to describe how particular factors change over time. For example, replacing the existing heart and blood vessel disease risk model with a newer or different population risk model can easily be done.
